procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the Patna High Court dated October 30, 1967, dismissing a criminal revision application.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a criminal revision application in the Patna High Court challenging the judgment of the First Additional Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi dated July 31, 1967, which had upheld the conviction and sentence passed by the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Ranchi. The High Court dismissed the revision application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the Patna High Court's judgment and order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the defamatory imputation made by the appellant was protected by the Ninth Exception, on the grounds that it was made in good faith for the protection of his interest in a proceeding under Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: In a proceeding under Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code concerning who was in possession of a piece of land, the appellant made a statement describing the respondent and his brother as 'illegitimate sons... born of a concubine'.
The appellant was convicted of defamation under Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code.
The appellant appealed, arguing that his statement was protected by the Ninth Exception to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code.
law: The Ninth Exception to Section 499 protects a defamatory imputation if it is made (1) in good faith and (2) for the protection of the interest of the person making it, another person, or for the public good.

To establish 'good faith', the accused must prove they acted with 'due care and attention'. This requires showing that they made an enquiry before making the statement and had a rational, objective basis to be satisfied that the imputation was true, not just a simple or blind belief.

To establish 'protection of interest', the accused must show that the imputation itself was for the protection of their interest. The mere existence of a legal proceeding does not give a person the right to make any defamatory statement they wish.
application: The Court first examined the requirement of 'good faith' and found that the appellant had presented no evidence to show that he had made any enquiry before making the imputation. Therefore, he failed to demonstrate that he had acted with the necessary 'due care and attention'.

The Court then analyzed the 'protection of interest' requirement. It determined that the legal proceeding was about land possession. The appellant's statement about the respondent's parentage was not relevant to protecting his interest in that possession dispute.
The Court explicitly stated that a person cannot resist a possession claim 'by hurling defamatory invectives and then claim the benefit of protection of interest'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, holding that his defamatory statement was not protected by the Ninth Exception because he failed to satisfy its two essential ingredients. He did not prove that the statement was made in good faith (as he made no prior enquiry), nor did he establish that the imputation was actually for the protection of his interest in the land possession proceeding.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the defamatory imputation made by the appellant was protected by the Ninth Exception, on the grounds that it was made in good faith for the protection of his interest in a proceeding under Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: The statements made in the written statement were true.
The disclosure was necessary to protect his interest in the property, which the respondent and his brother were dishonestly claiming.
The statement was made in a pending legal proceeding (under Section 144 CrPC) and was therefore justified for the protection of his interest.
respondent_arguments: The defamatory statement about legitimacy was not relevant to the proceeding under Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which was concerned with possession of the land, not title.
The appellant did not act in good faith, as he made no enquiry and did not show due care and attention before making the imputation.

Simply having a pending proceeding does not give a person the right to make defamatory statements; the imputation itself must be for the protection of the person's interest, which was not established here.

cases.case_name: Harbhajan Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the tests to determine whether the findings of fact (specifically, the absence of a good faith enquiry and lack of due care and attention before making an imputation) are sufficient to deny the benefit of the Ninth Exception to s. 499 IPC.

cases.case_name: Chaman Lal v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: For the legal standard required to establish 'good faith' under the Ninth Exception to section 499 of the Indian Penal Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To claim the defense of 'protection of interest' against a defamation charge, it is not sufficient that the statement was made during a pending legal proceeding concerning that interest. The person making the imputation must establish that they acted in good faith, which requires showing due care and enquiry, and that the specific imputation itself was for the protection of their interest.
obiter: "A. a shopkeeper, says to B. who manages his business-"Sell nothing to Z unless he pays you ready money, for I have no opinion of his honesty". A is within the exception, if he has made this imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests".

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant failed to establish the two essential ingredients of the Ninth Exception to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code. First, he could not prove he acted in 'good faith' because the findings of fact showed he made no enquiry and did not act with due care and attention before making the defamatory imputation. Second, he failed to show the imputation was for the 'protection of his interest' because the statement about the respondent's legitimacy was irrelevant to the actual issue in the Section 144 CrPC proceeding, which was concerned with possession of land, not title.
legal_tests_applied: The ingredients of the Ninth Exception are first that the imputation must be made in good faith; secondly, the imputation must be for protection of the interest of the person making it or of any other person or for the public good.

To establish 'good faith', a person must show they acted with due care and attention. Simple or actual belief is not enough; the belief must have a rational basis, which requires establishing as a fact that an enquiry was made before the imputation.

To establish 'protection of interest', the imputation itself must be for the protection of the interest of the person making it. The communication must be made bona fide upon a subject in which the person making it has an interest or duty, and the recipient has a corresponding interest or duty.

The test for good faith from Chaman Lal v. State of Punjab requires examining: (1) the circumstances of the statement; (2) the presence of malice; (3) whether an enquiry was made; (4) whether the person acted with care and caution; and (5) the preponderance of probability that the person acted in good faith.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to prove he acted in good faith, as there was no evidence he made any enquiry before the imputation, and he did not show due care and attention.

The appellant failed to show that the defamatory imputation was for the protection of his interest. The question in the Section 144 CrPC proceeding was about possession of land, and hurling defamatory invectives about legitimacy was not a valid way to resist a claim of possession.
The mere fact that a legal proceeding is pending does not give a person a license to make defamatory statements of this nature.
Even if the question of title had been involved, that in itself would not entitle a person to make a defamatory statement and then claim it was for the protection of their interest.
why_respondent_won: The appellant could not discharge the burden of proving the factual elements of the Ninth Exception, specifically good faith and the necessity of the statement for the protection of his interest.
The defamatory statement was found to be irrelevant to the legal proceeding in which it was made, as the proceeding concerned possession, not the respondent's parentage or title to the property.
The court accepted the findings of fact that the appellant did not act with care and caution and made no enquiry before making the imputation, which negated his claim of good faith.
policy_considerations: A pending legal proceeding cannot be used as a shield to make irrelevant and defamatory statements. The law does not permit a person to 'hurl defamatory invectives' and then claim the benefit of an exception meant to protect legitimate interests.

The protection of interest under the Ninth Exception is not an unlimited right; the defamatory statement itself must be shown to be the means of protecting that interest, and it must be relevant to the matter at hand.
